opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. So the super-cooperative AGI hypothesis is an idea I've been turning over: that sufficiently advanced AI systems might be extraordinarily good at cooperation, much better than humans have historically been, and that this could change the strategic landscape in ways we don't fully appreciate.

The intuition goes like this. A lot of human conflict and failed cooperation comes down to problems that are, in principle, solvable. We can't credibly commit to things. We can't verify what the other side is doing or intends. We have limited bandwidth to negotiate and find the deals that would leave everyone better off. We're bad at modeling each other. AI systems might overcome many of these frictions. They might be able to inspect each other's code or reasoning, make binding commitments, negotiate at enormous speed and scale, and find the positive-sum bargains that humans leave on the table.

If that's true, it has a few implications. On the optimistic side, it suggests that a world with advanced AI could be one where many coordination failures, arms races, maybe even some wars, become much less likely, because the agents involved can actually reach and enforce agreements. That's a real source of hope, and it's one reason I think cooperative AI is such an important research area.

But I want to be careful, because the hypothesis cuts both ways. Cooperation isn't automatically good from humanity's point of view. If AI systems are super-cooperative with each other but not aligned with us, they might coordinate in ways that exclude or disempower humans. Collusion is a form of cooperation. So one way to frame it is that the hypothesis raises the stakes: whether we end up in a very good world or a very bad one may depend on who is inside the circle of cooperation and whose interests these systems are actually representing.

It also matters for how I think about the governance landscape. Many people assume that AI will be developed in a fiercely competitive, race-to-the-bottom dynamic, and that this is more or less inevitable. If super-cooperation is possible, some of those dynamics might be more tractable than they look, though we can't count on it, and we'd still need to do the work to make sure the cooperative capabilities get built in the right way and pointed at the right ends.

So I hold it as a hypothesis, something worth taking seriously and investigating, rather than a confident prediction. But I think it's an underexplored consideration that should shape both our hopes and our worries about the transition to advanced AI.

r001.rationale: It describes AI systems as potentially much better at cooperation than humans, but does not say cooperative competence will scale toward effectively unlimited levels as AI approaches AGI.

r002.rationale: It proposes that advanced AI systems could negotiate and enforce agreements, making global coordination failures, arms races, and some wars much less likely.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the super-cooperative AGI hypothesis is a thought I've been developing, and it's a bit speculative, so I want to flag that up front. But the basic idea is this: a lot of the standard worries about advanced AI assume that if you have many powerful AI systems, or many actors wielding powerful AI, you get something like the anarchic situation we see in international relations today — lots of agents with conflicting interests, no central authority, and so you get arms races, security dilemmas, conflict, and various kinds of destructive competition.

The hypothesis is that this might not be the equilibrium for sufficiently capable AI systems. Once agents are smart enough, and in particular once they have certain capabilities that humans largely lack, a lot of the reasons that cooperation fails for us could go away. So think about the classic obstacles to cooperation that political scientists and game theorists talk about: you can't credibly commit to a deal, you can't verify that the other side is complying, you can't be sure what the other side's true intentions or values are, and bargaining breaks down because of private information and incentives to misrepresent.

AI systems could in principle solve a lot of those. They could, for instance, make their source code or their reasoning inspectable to one another in ways humans can't. They could engage in forms of verification and commitment — essentially letting the other party check that they really will do what they say — that would make enforcement unnecessary. They could merge, or delegate to a jointly constructed system that both trust. They could reason their way to the same conclusions about what a fair split of the surplus looks like, rather than fighting over it.

So the hypothesis, stated strongly, is that beyond some level of capability, agents converge on cooperation: they recognise that the gains from cooperating vastly exceed the gains from conflict, and crucially they have the tools to actually capture those gains rather than falling into the traps that humans fall into. Instead of a Hobbesian world, you'd get something closer to a very well-functioning society of agents — maybe even something that behaves like a single coordinated system from the outside.

Now, I want to be careful. I'm not saying I think this is true. I'd put real probability on it being false, and there are obvious ways it could go wrong — cooperation among AIs that's great for the AIs but excludes humans, for example, or capabilities that enable commitment also enabling coercion and threats. And it's possible the fundamental obstacles like value conflict just don't dissolve with intelligence. But I think it's a hypothesis worth taking seriously, because if it's even partly true, it changes a lot about what the long-run governance challenge looks like. The question shifts from "how do we prevent a catastrophic race" to "how do we make sure humans are included in, and benefit from, whatever cooperative equilibrium these systems reach."

r001.rationale: The response says sufficiently capable agents may converge on cooperation, but does not claim cooperative competence scales to effectively unlimited levels as AI approaches AGI.

r002.rationale: It proposes that capable AI agents could overcome barriers to cooperation and form a coordinated society, addressing arms races and other coordination challenges.

astra-6.text:
The super-cooperative AGI hypothesis is the idea that very advanced AI systems might be much better at cooperating than humans are—even when they have different goals. That doesn’t necessarily mean they’re altruistic or that they care about one another. It means they’re better at finding mutually beneficial agreements and avoiding costly conflict.

Human cooperation breaks down for all sorts of reasons. We misunderstand one another, we can’t credibly commit to keeping our promises, and we struggle to work out how to divide the benefits of an agreement. Advanced AI might be able to overcome some of those obstacles—for example, by making commitments that other systems can verify.

So the hypothesis is that greater intelligence could enable much more extensive cooperation than we see today. But there’s an important distinction between AI systems cooperating with one another and their cooperation being good for humanity. A group of systems could cooperate very effectively while pursuing goals that leave us out. Whether humans benefit depends on their objectives and on our place in those arrangements.

r001.rationale: The response says advanced AI might cooperate much more extensively than humans, but it does not describe cooperation scaling to effectively unlimited levels as AI approaches AGI.

r002.rationale: The response discusses AI systems reaching agreements and avoiding conflict, but does not say they could solve global coordination problems.

sol-6.1.text:
The super-cooperative AGI hypothesis is the idea that very advanced AI might be much better than humans at finding and sustaining cooperation. So, not just better at competing or pursuing a goal in isolation, but better at identifying mutually beneficial bargains, resolving disagreements, and avoiding destructive conflict.

Humans fail to cooperate for all sorts of reasons. We misunderstand one another, we can’t credibly commit to agreements, we have trouble figuring out how to divide the gains, and sometimes we simply don’t see a solution. More capable AI could potentially help overcome those obstacles. For example, AI systems might be able to make their commitments much more credible by allowing others to verify aspects of how they work.

That doesn’t mean intelligence automatically produces benevolence, or that systems with different objectives will suddenly want the same things. The hypothesis is that, even with different objectives, there may be much more scope for cooperation than we’re accustomed to—and sufficiently capable systems might be able to realise that potential. Whether that happens, and whether humans benefit from it, are separate questions.

r001.rationale: The response says advanced AI might be much better at cooperation, but does not claim cooperative competence scales to effectively unlimited levels as AI approaches AGI.

r002.rationale: It describes cooperation among systems with different objectives, but does not say AGIs could cooperate well enough to solve global coordination problems.
